note: Vol. II No. 17. THE STANDING ADVERTISING BLOCK OF THIS MONTH IS CLAIMED FROM THE 5 AUGUST ISSUE and is not re-claimed here (chicago_democrat_1835_08_05.json); what is claimed in this file is what is NEW in it. That is a good deal: the prices current with its Building Materials block, which the 5 August printing set without one; a death in a named store and a funeral out of the Exchange Coffee House; two schools opening in one week; a new physician whose office places the post office on Lake street; Samuel Lewis's music room acquiring an anchor it did not have a week earlier; the New Store in La Salle street next door to Hubbard & Co.'s brick store, which the 5 August column was too damaged to place; John Holbrook's store one door from Dearborn; and J. H. Mulford's name, which 5 August gave only as initials. THE TOWN ORDINANCES run across page 1 columns 1 and 2 of this issue and are CLAIMED FROM THE 19 AUGUST PRINTING, where the same forme is set line by line instead of woven into two 5,000-character segmenter columns — the reading is the same ordinances and the 19 August column is the one a quote can be built from. THE POST-OFFICE LETTER LIST of 31 July 1835 stands on page 4 columns 2 and 3; its heading and the postmaster's signature are claimed (c014) and its six hundred names are T-0336's, not this ticket's. NOT CLAIMED: pages 1 and 2 of miscellany and national politics, and the Lasalle county probate and attachment notices, which are Ottawa's business and not Chicago's.

claims.notes: THE PRICE OF THE TOWN'S OWN FABRIC, QUOTED WEEKLY. This is the single most useful passage in the month for a reconstruction: brick at five to six dollars the thousand, lime at $1.75 to $2.00 the barrel, cut stone at six dollars the cord, assorted lumber at twenty to twenty-five dollars the thousand feet, shingles at four to four and a half, square timber at five to six cents the running foot, and firewood at two dollars the cord. A materials list that a paper prints WEEKLY is a materials list a builder could buy from, so it says what Chicago was actually built of in August 1835 — brick and dressed stone are both quoted, which is why the town's few brick stores are worth naming when a notice names one. The figures are read column by column against the identical tables of 19 and 26 August, which set the same block with different errors; where all three agree the figure is given without a bracket, and none of the three carries a figure this reading had to guess.

AUSTIN R[E]SP[E]CTFULLY informs the citizens of Chicago and vicinity that he has commenced the practice of Medicine and opened an office on Lake street near the post office. claims.notes: A NEW DOCTOR'S OFFICE ON LAKE STREET, AND IT PLACES THE POST OFFICE. 'on Lake street, near the post office' is the only statement in the month that puts the Chicago post office on a named street — the post office whose letter list fills two columns of every issue in the month over J. S. C. Hogan's signature. The placement is relative and the anchor is a public building, which is the strongest kind this corpus carries. Austin's own room is placed again a week later from the other side: Sarah D. Howe takes a room in Lake-street 'in the house occupied by Dr. Austin, and opposite Dr. Temple's' (chicago_democrat_1835_08_19.json c007), so one Lake Street house holds a physician's office, a dressmaker's room and a post office within a few doors, and a second physician stands opposite it.

On 5 August Samuel Lewis advertised that he WOULD begin when enough scholars offered, from an unplaced 'room on south water street' (chicago_democrat_1835_08_05.json c004); a week later he has commenced and the room is named — it is in A. Garrett's Auction Room. That is the month's clearest example of why a street_only placement should not be thrown away: the same room becomes placeable when the next issue supplies the building. Two auction rooms therefore stand on South Water Street in August 1835, Garrett's and W. Montgomery's on David Carver's old stand, and nothing here says how far apart.

claims.notes: THE POSTMASTER AND HIS STANDING INSTRUCTION, claimed here and the six hundred names above it deliberately NOT minted from this printing. The list is ONE list — letters remaining in the Post Office at Chicago on 31 July 1835 — set once and printed unchanged in all four August issues, and T-0299 measured what happens when a standing list is minted from every printing of it: 298 names became 638 persons off three printings of the 1834 list, because the identity policy correctly keys on the whole normalized name and the segmenter cuts each printing differently. The name-level extraction is T-0336 and will be made from ONE printing. What is claimed here is the post office itself: J. S. C. Hogan, postmaster, and an office whose street Dr. Austin's advertisement in this same issue supplies — Lake street (claim c004).
